claim: Cell-free TX-TL systems prepared from E. coli extract can preserve the endogenous E. coli transcription machinery.
source: Cell-free expression systems prepared from an E. coli extract ('TX-TL') can preserve the endogenous E. coli transcription machinery as well as native mRNA and protein degradation mechanisms (Shin and Noireaux, 2010a; 2010b; 2012; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Shin and Noireaux, 2010a; 2010b; 2012; Sun et al., 2013)

claim: Cell-free TX-TL systems prepared from E. coli extract can preserve native mRNA and protein degradation mechanisms.
source: Cell-free expression systems prepared from an E. coli extract ('TX-TL') can preserve the endogenous E. coli transcription machinery as well as native mRNA and protein degradation mechanisms (Shin and Noireaux, 2010a; 2010b; 2012; Sun et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Shin and Noireaux, 2010a; 2010b; 2012; Sun et al., 2013)

claim: A microfluidic nano-reactor device is capable of emulating cellular growth and division.
source: We have recently described a microfluidic nano-reactor device capable of emulating cellular growth and division.
evidence: Authors reference their own recent work describing the device

claim: A discontinuous flow of TX-TL reagents through miniaturized reactors at rates matching natural E. coli dilution rates keeps transcription and translation rates at constant steady state levels.
source: A discontinuous flow of TX-TL reagents through miniaturized reactors at rates matching natural E. coli dilution rates keeps transcription and translation rates at constant steady state levels and removes reaction products, which is critical for the implementation of dynamic genetic networks (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013)

claim: Removing reaction products is critical for the implementation of dynamic genetic networks in cell-free systems.
source: A discontinuous flow of TX-TL reagents through miniaturized reactors at rates matching natural E. coli dilution rates keeps transcription and translation rates at constant steady state levels and removes reaction products, which is critical for the implementation of dynamic genetic networks (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013)

claim: Linear DNA can be used in lieu of plasmid DNA in TX-TL systems.
source: Linear DNA can be used in lieu of plasmid DNA, and the DNA source does not require specific compatible origins of replication or antibiotic markers.
evidence: Direct statement about the capability of the TX-TL system

claim: DNA used in TX-TL systems does not require specific compatible origins of replication or antibiotic markers.
source: Linear DNA can be used in lieu of plasmid DNA, and the DNA source does not require specific compatible origins of replication or antibiotic markers.
evidence: Direct statement about the requirements of DNA in TX-TL systems

claim: DNA can be assembled completely in vitro based on premade modules within 3 hr.
source: Therefore, DNA can be assembled completely in vitro based on premade modules within 3 hr (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Sun et al., 2014)

claim: The time needed for DNA assembly does not scale with circuit complexity in TX-TL systems.
source: Importantly, the time needed does not scale with circuit complexity, as each circuit component can be added as a separate linear template, which can be easily replaced or varied in concentration in following design-build-test cycles.
evidence: Logical inference from the modular nature of linear DNA assembly

claim: Prototyping a genetic circuit in TX-TL requires 4 to 78 hr.
source: We estimate that prototyping a genetic circuit in TX-TL requires 4 to 78 hr, as opposed to prototyping in E. coli, which requires a minimum of 52 hr to several weeks.
evidence: Estimate provided by authors and shown in Figure 1 bottom panel

claim: Prototyping a genetic circuit in E. coli requires a minimum of 52 hr to several weeks.
source: We estimate that prototyping a genetic circuit in TX-TL requires 4 to 78 hr, as opposed to prototyping in E. coli, which requires a minimum of 52 hr to several weeks.
evidence: Estimate provided by authors and shown in Figure 1 bottom panel

claim: The original repressilator network was successfully implemented in the cell-free system.
source: We successfully implemented the original repressilator network in our cell-free system and observed long-term sustained oscillations with periods matching the in vivo study (Figure 2, Video 1).
evidence: Experimental observation reported by authors and shown in Figure 2 and Video 1

claim: The original repressilator network in the cell-free system showed long-term sustained oscillations.
source: We successfully implemented the original repressilator network in our cell-free system and observed long-term sustained oscillations with periods matching the in vivo study (Figure 2, Video 1).
evidence: Experimental observation reported by authors and shown in Figure 2 and Video 1

claim: The oscillation periods of the repressilator in the cell-free system matched the in vivo study.
source: We successfully implemented the original repressilator network in our cell-free system and observed long-term sustained oscillations with periods matching the in vivo study (Figure 2, Video 1).
evidence: Experimental observation reported by authors and shown in Figure 2 and Video 1

claim: The OR2* mutation increases the repressor concentration necessary for half-maximal repression (K).
source: This mutation increases the repressor concentration necessary for half-maximal repression (K), and reduces cooperativity (Rosenfeld et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Rosenfeld et al., 2005)

claim: The OR2* mutation reduces cooperativity.
source: This mutation increases the repressor concentration necessary for half-maximal repression (K), and reduces cooperativity (Rosenfeld et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Rosenfeld et al., 2005)

claim: At long dilution times both the original repressilator and OR2* version oscillated.
source: At long dilution times (td) both circuits oscillated, but with shifted absolute reporter protein concentrations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2B

claim: The original repressilator and OR2* version oscillated with shifted absolute reporter protein concentrations at long dilution times.
source: At long dilution times (td) both circuits oscillated, but with shifted absolute reporter protein concentrations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2B

claim: At decreasing dilution times, repressilator amplitudes decreased.
source: At decreasing dilution times amplitudes decreased and periods became faster with a linear dependence on td.
evidence: Experimental observation from repressilator characterization

claim: At decreasing dilution times, repressilator periods became faster with a linear dependence on td.
source: At decreasing dilution times amplitudes decreased and periods became faster with a linear dependence on td.
evidence: Experimental observation from repressilator characterization

claim: Faster dilution times did not support oscillations for the modified OR2* network.
source: Faster dilution times, however, did not support oscillations for the modified network (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: The range of dilution times supporting oscillations can serve as a measure for robust oscillator function.
source: Experimentally, the range of dilution times supporting oscillations can serve as a measure for robust oscillator function, which generally diminishes with decreasing synthesis rates or when binding of one repressor to its promoter is weakened as in the OR2* mutant (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Experimental observation and inference supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3

claim: Robust oscillator function generally diminishes with decreasing synthesis rates.
source: Experimentally, the range of dilution times supporting oscillations can serve as a measure for robust oscillator function, which generally diminishes with decreasing synthesis rates or when binding of one repressor to its promoter is weakened as in the OR2* mutant (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Experimental observation and inference supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3

claim: Robust oscillator function generally diminishes when binding of one repressor to its promoter is weakened.
source: Experimentally, the range of dilution times supporting oscillations can serve as a measure for robust oscillator function, which generally diminishes with decreasing synthesis rates or when binding of one repressor to its promoter is weakened as in the OR2* mutant (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: Experimental observation and inference supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–3

claim: Initial conditions can influence the dynamic behavior of nonlinear systems.
source: Initial conditions can influence the dynamic behavior of nonlinear systems but are difficult to control in cells.
evidence: General knowledge about nonlinear systems

claim: Initial conditions are difficult to control in cells.
source: Initial conditions can influence the dynamic behavior of nonlinear systems but are difficult to control in cells.
evidence: General knowledge about experimental limitations in cellular systems

claim: For all initial conditions tested, the repressilator system quickly approached limit cycle oscillations.
source: For all conditions tested the system quickly approached limit cycle oscillations and was invariant to initial conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2D

claim: The repressilator system was invariant to initial conditions.
source: For all conditions tested the system quickly approached limit cycle oscillations and was invariant to initial conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 2D

claim: The repressilator network is symmetric in terms of transfer functions.
source: We measured the transfer functions of repressor-promoter pairs in the repressilator network (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3, Figure 3—source data 1) and found that the network is symmetric in terms of transfer functions.
evidence: Experimental measurement and analysis shown in Figure 3A and supplements

claim: In the CI promoter OR2* mutant, there was an expected shift in K value.
source: In the CI promoter OR2* mutant we observed the expected shift in K value and decreased steepness of the transfer function.
evidence: Experimental observation consistent with expectations

claim: In the CI promoter OR2* mutant, there was decreased steepness of the transfer function.
source: In the CI promoter OR2* mutant we observed the expected shift in K value and decreased steepness of the transfer function.
evidence: Experimental observation

claim: With the exception of QacR, TetR repressor homologs showed similar transfer functions as observed in vivo.
source: We also characterized TetR repressor homologs as building blocks for novel negative feedback circuits (Figure 3A) and with the exception of QacR observed similar transfer functions as observed in vivo (Stanton et al., 2014) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Experimental observation compared to in vivo data from Stanton et al., 2014, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: A novel 3-node ring oscillator (3n1) constructed on plasmid DNA showed high-amplitude oscillations over a broad range of dilution times.
source: Using three new repressors, BetI, PhlF and SrpR, we constructed a novel 3-node (3n) circuit, 3n1, and observed high-amplitude oscillations over a broad range of dilution times with the same dependence of amplitude and period on td as for the repressilator (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3B

claim: The 3n1 oscillator showed the same dependence of amplitude and period on td as the repressilator.
source: Using three new repressors, BetI, PhlF and SrpR, we constructed a novel 3-node (3n) circuit, 3n1, and observed high-amplitude oscillations over a broad range of dilution times with the same dependence of amplitude and period on td as for the repressilator (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3B

claim: Dilution rates are critical for the existence, period and amplitude of oscillations in the repressilator network and 3n1 oscillator.
source: In our characterization of the repressilator network and the 3n1 oscillator we found dilution rates to be critical for the existence, period and amplitude of oscillations.
evidence: Experimental finding from characterization studies

claim: Protein degradation is similar to dilution in that it results in removal of repressor proteins.
source: Protein degradation is similar to dilution in that it results in removal of repressor proteins.
evidence: Logical inference based on the mechanisms of protein removal

claim: Oscillations were observed for both versions of the 3n2 circuit (with and without ssrA-tags).
source: We observed oscillations for both circuits (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3C

claim: The 3n2 circuit without ssrA-tag mediated protein degradation exhibited slower oscillations.
source: However, the circuit without ssrA-tag mediated protein degradation exhibited slower oscillations, which extended to lower dilution times, showing that protein degradation, just like dilution, affects oscillator function and period.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3C

claim: Protein degradation affects oscillator function and period.
source: However, the circuit without ssrA-tag mediated protein degradation exhibited slower oscillations, which extended to lower dilution times, showing that protein degradation, just like dilution, affects oscillator function and period.
evidence: Experimental observation and inference from Figure 3C

claim: ClpXP-mediated protein degradation has been shown to be important for existence and frequency of oscillations in vivo.
source: Effects of ClpXP-mediated protein degradation, which have been shown to be important for existence and frequency of oscillations in vivo (Cookson et al., 2011; Prindle et al., 2014), can thus be emulated in a cell-free environment.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Cookson et al., 2011; Prindle et al., 2014)

claim: Effects of ClpXP-mediated protein degradation can be emulated in a cell-free environment.
source: Effects of ClpXP-mediated protein degradation, which have been shown to be important for existence and frequency of oscillations in vivo (Cookson et al., 2011; Prindle et al., 2014), can thus be emulated in a cell-free environment.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations of 3n2 circuit variants

claim: Theory predicts that ring architectures built from an odd number of repressors oscillate.
source: Theory predicts that ring architectures built from an odd number of repressors oscillate, while even-numbered architectures have stable steady states (Smith, 1987; Hori et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work (Smith, 1987; Hori et al., 2013)

claim: Theory predicts that even-numbered ring architectures have stable steady states.
source: Theory predicts that ring architectures built from an odd number of repressors oscillate, while even-numbered architectures have stable steady states (Smith, 1987; Hori et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work (Smith, 1987; Hori et al., 2013)

claim: Initial pulses of IPTG or aTc allowed switching of the 4-node circuit expression into either one of two stable steady states.
source: Initial pulses of LacI inducer IPTG or TetR inducer aTc allowed us to switch expression into either one of the two stable steady states (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3D

claim: Stable steady states in the 4-node circuit were reached after an initial adjustment phase of 5 to 10 hr.
source: Stable steady states were reached after an initial adjustment phase of 5 to 10 hr and remained stable until the experiment was terminated after 22 hr.
evidence: Experimental observation from 4-node circuit experiments

claim: Stable steady states in the 4-node circuit remained stable until the experiment was terminated after 22 hr.
source: Stable steady states were reached after an initial adjustment phase of 5 to 10 hr and remained stable until the experiment was terminated after 22 hr.
evidence: Experimental observation from 4-node circuit experiments

claim: Non-oscillating networks function in the cell-free environment.
source: These results show that non-oscillating networks also function in the cell-free environment and that the oscillations we observe for the 3-node networks are determined by network architecture and not established by particular reaction conditions in the microfluidic reactor.
evidence: Inference from the 4-node bistable switch experimental results

claim: The oscillations observed for the 3-node networks are determined by network architecture and not by particular reaction conditions in the microfluidic reactor.
source: These results show that non-oscillating networks also function in the cell-free environment and that the oscillations we observe for the 3-node networks are determined by network architecture and not established by particular reaction conditions in the microfluidic reactor.
evidence: Inference from comparing oscillating 3-node and non-oscillating 4-node circuits

claim: Both 5-node ring networks (5n1 and 5n2) oscillated over a broad range of dilution times.
source: Despite their considerable complexity both circuits indeed oscillated over a broad range of dilution times.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3E

claim: The period of the 5n networks (up to 19 hr) was significantly longer than that of the 3n networks (up to 8 hr).
source: The period of the 5n networks (up to 19 hr) was significantly longer than that of the 3n networks (up to 8 hr).
evidence: Experimental observation from comparing 3n and 5n networks

claim: The observed periods of all ssrA-tagged 3n and 5n ring architectures could be accurately predicted by computational simulations.
source: Comparing all ssrA-tagged 3n and 5n ring architectures, we show that the observed periods could be accurately predicted for all four networks by computational simulations (Figure 3F).
evidence: Comparison of experimental data with computational predictions shown in Figure 3F

claim: Both 3n oscillators (3n1 and 3n2) showed regular oscillations with periods of 6 ± 1 hr for at least 30 hr in E. coli.
source: When tested on a microfluidic device (mother machine (Wang et al., 2010)), both 3n oscillators showed regular oscillations with periods of 6 ± 1 hr for at least 30 hr (Figure 4A, Videos 2,3).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4A and Videos 2,3

claim: All cells undergoing healthy cellular division oscillated for both 3n oscillators (n=71).
source: Both oscillators were surprisingly robust as all cells undergoing healthy cellular division oscillated (n=71) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 4).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Video 4

claim: 5n1 with a high expression-strength reporter caused slow growth and high cell death rates when run on the mother machine.
source: Specifically, 5n1 with a high expression-strength reporter caused slow growth and high cell death rates when run on the mother machine – we hypothesize that this is due to loading effects from high protein production, as decreasing the reporter expression strength resolved cell viability issues (Ceroni et al., 2015).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli

claim: Decreasing the reporter expression strength resolved cell viability issues for 5n1.
source: Specifically, 5n1 with a high expression-strength reporter caused slow growth and high cell death rates when run on the mother machine – we hypothesize that this is due to loading effects from high protein production, as decreasing the reporter expression strength resolved cell viability issues (Ceroni et al., 2015).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli, with citation to related work (Ceroni et al., 2015)

claim: Both 5n oscillators showed robust oscillations in E. coli that were maintained for at least 70 hr.
source: When tested with a low expression-strength reporter both 5n oscillators showed robust oscillations in E. coli that were maintained for at least 70 hr, and over 95% of all analyzed traps containing healthy cells oscillated (n=104).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4B

claim: Over 95% of all analyzed traps containing healthy cells oscillated for the 5n oscillators (n=104).
source: When tested with a low expression-strength reporter both 5n oscillators showed robust oscillations in E. coli that were maintained for at least 70 hr, and over 95% of all analyzed traps containing healthy cells oscillated (n=104).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: 5n1 oscillated with a period of 8 hr in E. coli.
source: In addition, both 5n networks oscillated with similar periods: 8 hr for 5n1, and 9 hr for 5n2 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Videos 5–7).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: 5n2 oscillated with a period of 9 hr in E. coli.
source: In addition, both 5n networks oscillated with similar periods: 8 hr for 5n1, and 9 hr for 5n2 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Videos 5–7).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Starting from a single cell, striking oscillation pulses of the entire growing microcolony were observed for both 3n oscillators on a CellASIC system.
source: We also tested both 3n oscillators on a CellASIC system, which allows planar single-layer colony formation. Starting from a single cell we observed striking oscillation pulses of the entire growing microcolony (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Videos 8,9).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and Videos 8,9

claim: Population level pulses were apparent when using three different fluorescent reporters simultaneously for 3n oscillators.
source: These population level pulses were also apparent when using three different fluorescent reporters simultaneously (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, Video 10).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Video 10

claim: Population level oscillations were not observed in the original repressilator.
source: We did not observe population level oscillations in either the original repressilator, the OR2* mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) or the 5n networks.
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: Population level oscillations were not observed in the OR2* mutant.
source: We did not observe population level oscillations in either the original repressilator, the OR2* mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) or the 5n networks.
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: Population level oscillations were not observed in the 5n networks.
source: We did not observe population level oscillations in either the original repressilator, the OR2* mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) or the 5n networks.
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli

claim: Synchronized oscillations were not reported with the original repressilator.
source: Synchronized oscillations were not reported with the original repressilator (Elowitz and Leibler, 2000), and have only been observed in oscillators using intercellular communication (Danino et al., 2010; Prindle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Elowitz and Leibler, 2000; Danino et al., 2010; Prindle et al., 2012)

claim: Synchronized oscillations have only been observed in oscillators using intercellular communication.
source: Synchronized oscillations were not reported with the original repressilator (Elowitz and Leibler, 2000), and have only been observed in oscillators using intercellular communication (Danino et al., 2010; Prindle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Danino et al., 2010; Prindle et al., 2012)

claim: The population-wide in-phase oscillations observed in 3n1 and 3n2 are not believed to be due to an active coupling mechanism.
source: In contrast to these quorum-sensing mechanisms that can actively couple and synchronize oscillator states (Danino et al., 2010; Prindle et al., 2012) we do not believe the population-wide in-phase oscillations we observed are due to an active coupling mechanism.
evidence: Authors' interpretation of their experimental observations

claim: The population-level oscillations of the 3n1 and 3n2 networks are hypothesized to be due to increased repressor concentrations as compared to the original repressilator network.
source: We hypothesize that the population-level oscillations of the 3n1 and 3n2 networks are due to increased repressor concentrations as compared to the original repressilator network, which increases the inheritance of the period phenotype and minimizes the rapid de-phasing expected from stochastic cellular protein fluctuations (Kiviet et al., 2014).
evidence: Authors' hypothesis based on experimental observations and citation to related work (Kiviet et al., 2014)

claim: A direct relationship was found between division times and period for 3n oscillators.
source: We varied dilution time by using different media conditions and media flow rates, and found a direct relationship between division times and period, consistent with the cell-free data collected.
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4D

claim: Oscillation periods of the 5n oscillators were consistent with cell-free results.
source: Oscillation periods of the 5n oscillators were also consistent with our cell-free results and showed a similar dependence on doubling time (Figure 4D).
evidence: Comparison of in vivo and in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Oscillation periods of the 5n oscillators showed a similar dependence on doubling time.
source: Oscillation periods of the 5n oscillators were also consistent with our cell-free results and showed a similar dependence on doubling time (Figure 4D).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4D

claim: Given a constant concentration of ClpXP, stronger reporters would result in more ClpXP loading, thereby slowing the period of oscillation.
source: We theorized that given a constant concentration of ClpXP, stronger reporters would result in more ClpXP loading, thereby slowing the period of oscillation.
evidence: Authors' theoretical reasoning about ClpXP loading effects

claim: ClpXP is thought to influence oscillation dynamics in vivo.
source: ClpXP is thought to influence oscillation dynamics in vivo in this manner (Cookson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Cookson et al., 2011)

claim: Both the period distributions of 3n1 and 5n2 showed that stronger reporters resulted in longer periods.
source: We found that in the mother machine, both the period distributions of 3n1 and 5n2 showed this characteristic (Figure 4E), which reflects our cell-free findings of differential –ssrA tag dependent period length (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli shown in Figure 4E

claim: The in vivo observation of reporter-dependent period length reflects cell-free findings of differential ssrA tag dependent period length.
source: We found that in the mother machine, both the period distributions of 3n1 and 5n2 showed this characteristic (Figure 4E), which reflects our cell-free findings of differential –ssrA tag dependent period length (Figure 3C).
evidence: Comparison of in vivo and in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 3C

claim: Synthetic dynamic networks can be readily implemented, characterized, and engineered in a cell-free system and subsequently transferred to cellular hosts.
source: We showed that synthetic dynamic networks can be readily implemented, characterized, and engineered in a cell-free system and subsequently transferred to cellular hosts (Figure 1).
evidence: Summary of experimental results demonstrated throughout the study

claim: The cell-free system resulted in the experimental validation of previous theoretical predictions on even- and odd-numbered cyclic negative feedback circuits.
source: The cell-free system resulted in the experimental validation of previous theoretical predictions on even- and odd-numbered cyclic negative feedback circuits (Smith, 1987; Hori et al., 2013) and enabled the in vivo implementation of robust 5-node genetic oscillators.
evidence: Summary of experimental results validating theoretical predictions from Smith, 1987 and Hori et al., 2013

claim: The cell-free system enabled the in vivo implementation of robust 5-node genetic oscillators.
source: The cell-free system resulted in the experimental validation of previous theoretical predictions on even- and odd-numbered cyclic negative feedback circuits (Smith, 1987; Hori et al., 2013) and enabled the in vivo implementation of robust 5-node genetic oscillators.
evidence: Summary of experimental results showing successful implementation of 5-node oscillators

claim: The cell-free environment can fill the gap between theoretical network design and in vivo implementation of biological systems.
source: The cell-free environment can thus fill the gap between theoretical network design and in vivo implementation of biological systems and provide a simplified and controlled environment that drastically reduces the design-build-test cycle (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference from the demonstrated utility of the cell-free approach, with citation to Sun et al., 2014

claim: The cell-free environment provides a simplified and controlled environment that drastically reduces the design-build-test cycle.
source: The cell-free environment can thus fill the gap between theoretical network design and in vivo implementation of biological systems and provide a simplified and controlled environment that drastically reduces the design-build-test cycle (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference from experimental results and citation to Sun et al., 2014

claim: Oscillation periods in negative feedback ring oscillators are mainly determined by degradation and dilution rates.
source: Oscillation periods in negative feedback ring oscillators are mainly determined by degradation and dilution rates (Hori et al., 2013), which explains the good correspondence between oscillation periods in our cell-free environment and in E. coli.
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work (Hori et al., 2013) and used to explain experimental observations

claim: There is good correspondence between oscillation periods in the cell-free environment and in E. coli.
source: Oscillation periods in negative feedback ring oscillators are mainly determined by degradation and dilution rates (Hori et al., 2013), which explains the good correspondence between oscillation periods in our cell-free environment and in E. coli.
evidence: Summary of experimental observations comparing in vitro and in vivo periods

claim: Almost all prototyping can be done on linear DNA, which requires less than 8 hr to assemble and test.
source: By constructing and testing novel network architectures we show that almost all prototyping can be done on linear DNA, which requires less than 8 hr to assemble and test.
evidence: Summary of experimental approach and timing demonstrated in the study

claim: Linear DNA allows rapid screening of different network topologies.
source: This allows rapid screening of different network topologies and rapid screening of parameters important for the desired function of a network.
evidence: Inference from the demonstrated utility of linear DNA in the study

claim: Linear DNA allows rapid screening of parameters important for the desired function of a network.
source: This allows rapid screening of different network topologies and rapid screening of parameters important for the desired function of a network.
evidence: Inference from the demonstrated utility of linear DNA in the study

claim: Some differences were observed between the cell-free and cellular environment, particularly in predicting cellular toxicity and loading effects of the 5n oscillators in vivo.
source: We observed some differences between the cell-free and cellular environment, particularly in the difficulty of predicting cellular toxicity and loading effects of the 5n oscillators in vivo, and some differences between promoter and repressor strengths.
evidence: Summary of observed limitations in the cell-free approach

claim: Some differences were observed between promoter and repressor strengths in the cell-free and cellular environment.
source: We observed some differences between the cell-free and cellular environment, particularly in the difficulty of predicting cellular toxicity and loading effects of the 5n oscillators in vivo, and some differences between promoter and repressor strengths.
evidence: Summary of observed differences between in vitro and in vivo systems

claim: 5n2 showed similar oscillations as compared to 5n1 when analyzed on linear DNA in the cell-free environment.
source: 5n2 showed similar oscillations as compared to 5n1 when analyzed on linear DNA in the cell-free environment (Figure 3E) and on plasmid DNA in E. coli (Figure 4), but we did not observe oscillations for 5n2 when run from the same plasmid DNA in the cell-free environment.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 3E

claim: 5n2 showed similar oscillations as compared to 5n1 when analyzed on plasmid DNA in E. coli.
source: 5n2 showed similar oscillations as compared to 5n1 when analyzed on linear DNA in the cell-free environment (Figure 3E) and on plasmid DNA in E. coli (Figure 4), but we did not observe oscillations for 5n2 when run from the same plasmid DNA in the cell-free environment.
evidence: Experimental observation shown in Figure 4

claim: Oscillations were not observed for 5n2 when run from plasmid DNA in the cell-free environment.
source: 5n2 showed similar oscillations as compared to 5n1 when analyzed on linear DNA in the cell-free environment (Figure 3E) and on plasmid DNA in E. coli (Figure 4), but we did not observe oscillations for 5n2 when run from the same plasmid DNA in the cell-free environment.
evidence: Experimental observation

claim: The lack of oscillations for 5n2 on plasmid DNA in the cell-free environment is hypothesized to be due to differences in expression efficiencies from linear and plasmid DNA in cell-free prototyping environments.
source: We hypothesize this is due to differences in expression efficiencies from linear and plasmid DNA in cell-free prototyping environments (Sun et al., 2014; Chappell et al., 2013), and/or differences between repressor strengths in the cell-free and the cellular environment (particularly for QacR, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Authors' hypothesis supported by citations to prior work (Sun et al., 2014; Chappell et al., 2013)

claim: The lack of oscillations for 5n2 on plasmid DNA in the cell-free environment is hypothesized to be due to differences between repressor strengths in the cell-free and the cellular environment.
source: We hypothesize this is due to differences in expression efficiencies from linear and plasmid DNA in cell-free prototyping environments (Sun et al., 2014; Chappell et al., 2013), and/or differences between repressor strengths in the cell-free and the cellular environment (particularly for QacR, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Authors' hypothesis based on experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: The observed behavior of complex networks in the cell-free environment reflected network behavior in vivo well.
source: While more work is necessary describing and explaining differences between in vitro and in vivo environments, the observed behavior of complex networks in our cell-free environment reflected network behavior in vivo well.
evidence: Summary of experimental results comparing in vitro and in vivo network behavior

claim: Cell-free systems are a powerful emulator of the cellular environment allowing precise control over experimental conditions.
source: Cell-free systems are thus a powerful emulator of the cellular environment allowing precise control over experimental conditions and enabling studies that are difficult or time consuming to perform in cells.
evidence: Inference from the demonstrated capabilities of the cell-free system throughout the study

claim: Cell-free systems enable studies that are difficult or time consuming to perform in cells.
source: Cell-free systems are thus a powerful emulator of the cellular environment allowing precise control over experimental conditions and enabling studies that are difficult or time consuming to perform in cells.
evidence: Inference from the demonstrated capabilities of the cell-free system throughout the study

claim: Cell-free systems will be useful for prototyping and characterizing novel synthetic systems.
source: We envision that it will not only be useful for prototyping and characterizing novel synthetic systems but also facilitate in-depth analyses of native biological networks in a simplified setting.
evidence: Authors' projection based on demonstrated utility in the study

claim: The cell-free approach is posed to play an increasing role in biological systems engineering.
source: With further developments in cell-free lysate systems and supporting technologies, the cell-free approach is posed to play an increasing role in biological systems engineering and provides a unique opportunity to design, build, and analyze biological systems.
evidence: Authors' projection about the future role of cell-free systems

claim: The cell-free approach provides a unique opportunity to design, build, and analyze biological systems.

claim: Performing extensive, quantitative and rapid network characterization in cells is limited due to difficulties associated with measuring parts, components, and systems in complex and ill-defined cellular hosts.
source: Performing extensive, quantitative and rapid network characterization in cells is limited due to difficulties associated with measuring parts, components, and systems in complex and ill-defined cellular hosts (Kwok, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Kwok, 2010)

claim: Lack of precise control over network component concentrations is a problem for characterizing biological networks in cells.
source: Particular problems include: I) lack of precise control over network component concentrations, II) unpredictable interactions and integration with host cell processes, III) cumbersome molecular cloning, and IV) technical challenges and limited throughput associated with single cell measurements.
evidence: General knowledge about limitations of cellular systems

source: Reconstituted biochemical systems have allowed the study of complex dynamic and self-organizing behaviors outside of cells such as switches, oscillators and pattern-forming regulatory networks (Schwille and Diez, 2009; Genot et al., 2013; van Roekel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Schwille and Diez, 2009; Genot et al., 2013; van Roekel et al., 2015)

claim: Networks assembled from simplified biochemistries such as oligonucleotide polymerization and degradation reactions can produce complex behaviors such as oscillations.
source: Networks assembled from simplified biochemistries such as oligonucleotide polymerization and degradation reactions can produce complex behaviors such as oscillations and provide insights into the working principles of biological regulatory systems (Genot et al., 2013; van Roekel et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Genot et al., 2013; van Roekel et al., 2015)

claim: A growing number of synthetic gene networks with increasing complexity have been implemented in cell-free transcription-translation systems.
source: A growing number of synthetic gene networks with increasing complexity have been implemented in cell-free transcription-translation systems (Noireaux et al., 2003; Shin and Noireaux, 2012; Takahashi et al., 2015; Pardee, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Noireaux et al., 2003; Shin and Noireaux, 2012; Takahashi et al., 2015; Pardee, 2014)

claim: Oscillating genetic networks can be implemented in vitro outside of cells using microfluidic devices.
source: We and others have recently shown that oscillating genetic networks can be implemented in vitro outside of cells using microfluidic devices (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013; Karzbrun et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent work (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013; Karzbrun et al., 2014)

claim: A few studies investigated whether individual components such as promoters and ribosomal binding sites express at comparable strengths in cell-free systems and in cells.
source: A few studies investigated whether individual components such as promoters and ribosomal binding sites express at comparable strengths in cell-free systems and in cells (Sun et al., 2014; Chappell et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Sun et al., 2014; Chappell et al., 2013)

claim: Comparisons of the behavior of genetic networks in cell-free systems and in cells are limited to a few examples such as repressor-promoter pairs and a RNA transcriptional repressor cascade.
source: Comparisons of the behavior of genetic networks in cell-free systems and in cells are still limited to a few examples such as repressor-promoter pairs (Chappell et al., 2013; Karig et al., 2012) and a RNA transcriptional repressor cascade (Takahashi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Chappell et al., 2013; Karig et al., 2012; Takahashi et al., 2015)

claim: It has not been shown whether genetic networks with complex dynamic behavior function similarly in cell-free and cellular environments prior to this study.
source: Thus far, however, it has not been shown whether genetic networks with complex dynamic behavior function similarly in cell-free and cellular environments.
evidence: Statement about the gap in knowledge that this study addresses

claim: Novel 3-node, 4-node, and 5-node negative feedback architectures were implemented and characterized in vitro.
source: Here, we demonstrate that cell-free systems can be used to characterize and engineer complex dynamic behaviors of genetic networks by implementing and characterizing novel 3-node, 4-node, and 5-node negative feedback architectures in vitro.
evidence: Summary of experimental work presented in the study

claim: The 3- and 5-node oscillator networks were functional in cells.
source: We go on to show that our 3- and 5-node oscillator networks were functional in cells and that their periods were comparable to those observed in the cell-free system, indicating that the cell-free system accurately emulated the cellular environment for the complex dynamic networks developed and tested in this study.
evidence: Summary of experimental results showing in vivo functionality

claim: The periods of 3- and 5-node oscillator networks in cells were comparable to those observed in the cell-free system.
source: We go on to show that our 3- and 5-node oscillator networks were functional in cells and that their periods were comparable to those observed in the cell-free system, indicating that the cell-free system accurately emulated the cellular environment for the complex dynamic networks developed and tested in this study.
evidence: Summary of experimental results comparing in vitro and in vivo periods

claim: The cell-free system accurately emulated the cellular environment for the complex dynamic networks developed and tested in this study.
source: We go on to show that our 3- and 5-node oscillator networks were functional in cells and that their periods were comparable to those observed in the cell-free system, indicating that the cell-free system accurately emulated the cellular environment for the complex dynamic networks developed and tested in this study.
evidence: Inference from the comparison of in vitro and in vivo experimental results

claim: Cells carrying the 3-node networks oscillated on a population level.
source: Cells carrying our 3-node networks oscillated on a population level, which was previously only observed in actively synchronized oscillators using quorum-based coupling (Danino et al., 2010).
evidence: Experimental observation in E. coli, with citation to prior work (Danino et al., 2010)

claim: Population-wide oscillations were previously only observed in actively synchronized oscillators using quorum-based coupling.
source: Cells carrying our 3-node networks oscillated on a population level, which was previously only observed in actively synchronized oscillators using quorum-based coupling (Danino et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Danino et al., 2010)

claim: The in vitro and in vivo oscillations of the 5-node negative feedback networks confirm theoretical predictions on biomolecular ring oscillators.
source: The in vitro and in vivo oscillations of our 5-node negative feedback networks confirm theoretical predictions on biomolecular ring oscillators and represent the largest synthetic negative feedback networks implemented simultaneously in cell-free systems and in cells.
evidence: Summary of experimental results validating theoretical predictions

claim: The 5-node negative feedback networks represent the largest synthetic negative feedback networks implemented simultaneously in cell-free systems and in cells.
source: The in vitro and in vivo oscillations of our 5-node negative feedback networks confirm theoretical predictions on biomolecular ring oscillators and represent the largest synthetic negative feedback networks implemented simultaneously in cell-free systems and in cells.

claim: TX-TL extract was prepared from strain JS006 co-transformed with Rosetta2 plasmid.
source: Preparation of TX-TL was conducted as described previously (Sun et al., 2013), but using strain 'JS006' co-transformed with Rosetta2 plasmid and performing a 1:2:1 extract:DNA:buffer ratio.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The TX-TL extract (eZS4) contained 8.7 mg/mL protein.
source: This resulted in extract 'eZS4' with: 8.7 mg/mL protein, 10.5 mM Mg-glutamate, 100 mM K-glutamate, 0.25 mM DTT, 0.75 mM each amino acid except leucine, 0.63 mM leucine, 50 mM HEPES, 1.5 mM ATP and GTP, 0.9 mM CTP and UTP, 0.2 mg/mL tRNA, 0.26 mM CoA, 0.33 mM NAD, 0.75 mM cAMP, 0.068 mM folinic acid, 1 mM spermidine, 30 mM 3-PGA, 2% PEG-8000.
evidence: Description of experimental composition

claim: Experiments were performed in a microfluidic nano-reactor device at a reaction temperature of 33°C.
source: Experiments were performed in a microfluidic nano-reactor device as described previously (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2013) with some modifications to optimize the conditions for the lysate-based TX-TL mix. Reaction temperature was 33°C.
evidence: Description of experimental conditions

claim: Experiments were run with dilution rates (µ) between approximately 2.8 and 0.5 hr-1.
source: We ran experiments with dilution rates (µ) between approximately 2.8 and 0.5 hr-1, which corresponds to dilution times, td = ln(2) µ-1, between 15 and 85 min.
evidence: Description of experimental parameters

claim: Maturation time of Cerulean was determined to be 15 ± 4 min.
source: Maturation times of Citrine and Cerulean were determined as described previously (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013) and were 15 ± 4 min for Cerulean and 29 ± 3 min for Citrine.
evidence: Experimental measurement

claim: Maturation time of Citrine was determined to be 29 ± 3 min.
source: Maturation times of Citrine and Cerulean were determined as described previously (Niederholtmeyer et al., 2013) and were 15 ± 4 min for Cerulean and 29 ± 3 min for Citrine.
evidence: Experimental measurement

claim: Mother machine experiments were conducted with E. coli cells trapped in channels of 30 µm length, 2 µm width and 1.2 µm height.
source: Mother machine (Wang et al., 2010) experiments were conducted with custom-made microfluidic chips (mold courtesy of M. Delincé and J. McKinney, EPFL). E. coli cells were trapped in channels of 30 µm length, 2 µm width and 1.2 µm height.
evidence: Description of experimental setup

claim: Mother machine experiments were performed using LB medium supplemented with 0.075% Tween-20 at a flow rate of 400 µl/hr.
source: Experiments were performed using LB medium supplemented with 0.075% Tween-20 at a flow rate of 400 µl/hr.
evidence: Description of experimental conditions

claim: Cells were imaged in time series every 10-20 min using a 100x phase objective.
source: Cells were imaged in time series every 10-–20 min using a 100x phase objective minimizing both lamp intensity (12% Xcite 120, Excelitas Inc. Waltam MA or 1–2% CoolLED pE-2, Custom interconnected Ltd., UK) and exposure times (<500 ms) to limit photo-toxicity.
